claim: Pre-use of an object in its usual role makes a new use harder: a filled box in the candle task is solved far less often than an empty box (about 2:1 in Adamson 1952; Glucksberg 1962 same direction). Both seen only through Wikipedia summaries, no N.
agent_test: Give the agent a candle-type task with the key object already 'used' in the prompt vs presented unused; measure solve rate at fixed tokens, with and without an O6 step that lists each object's alternative roles.

claim: Wording and layout alone change fixation in the written candle task: underlining the object nouns raised solving from 23% to 55% (Frank and Ramscar 2003; the Candle page says 25% to 50%); 'box and tacks' beats 'box of tacks' (Higgins and Chaires); tacks beside the box gives near-universal solving. Exact percentages differ between sources.
agent_test: Rewrite the same puzzles with noun-underlined vs plain vs 'X of Y' phrasing; check whether S1 (restating the problem with parts named separately) closes the gap on plain wording.

claim: High incentive worsens performance when the dominant habit is wrong (Glucksberg 1962 filled-box condition). One study seen, as summarised on Wikipedia; no N, no replication opened. Often over-generalised to 'incentives hurt creativity'.
agent_test: Not an agent claim; only a prompt-pressure probe (urgency wording) on fixation tasks would test it.

claim: Direction of prior use matters: after pretraining with one object (relay or switch) people use the other as pendulum weight (Maier 1930/31; Birch and Rabinowitz 1951). No N or counts opened.
agent_test: Prime the agent with one of two equivalent tools; check it picks the unprimed one, and whether S1 naming removes this.

claim: Functional fixedness is not clearly universal or developmental: Shuar adults showed it (German and Barrett 2005, called preliminary), 6-7 year olds show it, 4-5 year olds mixed, apes show weaker or non-significant effects (chimpanzee study 2024: success 5/8 vs 8/8, Fisher p=0.200; time measures significant).
agent_test: No direct agent test; use only as background that fixation is a learned-habit effect, so an agent with strong training priors should show it.

claim: A trained 'generic parts' technique (describe objects by parts, not names) raised solving of fixedness-affected problems by 67% relative (McCaffrey 2012). Single study, relative gain, no N seen, no independent replication.
agent_test: Add a generic-parts decomposition step to O6 and compare with plain at equal tokens on a candle/Duncker-type set.

claim: Einstellung (mechanised set) is real in humans: Luchins 1942 water-jar rigidity of 70% (no stress) and 98% (anxiety), extinction-problem failure 58% and 97%; also seen with experts in chess (Sheridan and Reingold 2013, N=34), anagrams (N=60) and chunk decomposition (N=32 and 28). Luchins numbers are from Wikipedia only. Update: the 483-children and 3-of-98 figures are on the current Wikipedia page (d01); primary Luchins 1942 still unopened.
agent_test: Build water-jar-style sequences (induce a set, then a simpler path); measure the rate at which the agent keeps the learned path.

claim: Einstellung costs speed more often than accuracy, and is weak when the familiar move is a blunder: anagram accuracy 51.7 vs 53.8% (n.s.) but 15.3 vs 13.4 s; chess problems 2-4 with a blunder familiar move showed little effect; chunk decomposition Exp 2 changed RT only (Exp 1 changed accuracy).
agent_test: Log tokens-to-solution as well as accuracy when testing set effects in the agent; accuracy alone can hide the cost.

claim: In chess, experts who still found the optimal move scanned more of the board (more dwells; F(1,15)=12.34) than experts who took the familiar move; the '3 SD drop' of Bilalic et al. 2008 is only cited, not verified.
agent_test: Check whether the agent that avoids the trap spends more tokens on alternative candidates (a behavioural proxy for the extra dwells).

claim: Incubation gives a small positive effect: Sio and Ormerod 2009 mean d=0.29 (117 studies), Strick 2011 g=0.224 (92 studies); a 4 min break helped as much as 12 min; sleep about doubled insight solutions (Wagner 2004, single lab). Moderators mixed; Vul and Pashler 2007 not verified.
agent_test: Compare a forced restart with fresh context (clean re-read) against continuing the same trace at equal tokens.

claim: Insight versus non-insight is a feature of the solver's experience, not the problem: Aha ratings predict accuracy for insight tasks (r=0.40-0.50) but not for non-insight (r=0.02-0.24); accuracy equal or lower for insight problems (0.45-0.51 vs 0.54-0.64).
agent_test: Not an agent test.

claim: Memory strength of the red-herring decoy sets the size of fixation (Beda and Smith 2018). Seen only as cited in Naeini et al.; primary not opened. Human dose evidence now exists: strong induction hurt only when the answer was weakly associated (N=30, d12); no LLM test.
agent_test: Vary how strongly a decoy association is primed in the prompt and check fixation size.

claim: LLMs are strongly blocked by red herrings: Only Connect walls (494 test): GPT-4 0-shot solved 6 walls (239 of 1976 groups) vs humans 285 (1405 groups). Removing herrings: OCW-Randomized 59 walls, OCW-WordNet 471 walls (97.5% of groups). More in-context examples did not help (GPT-4 6,4,5,7,3 walls at 0/1/3/5/10 shot; re-verified in the PDF). Confound: WordNet walls are also easier categories. One paper.
agent_test: Re-run with decoys removed vs present on our own wall set; test an O6 step that asks which clue could belong to two groups, at equal tokens; add chain-of-thought, which the authors did not run.

claim: LLMs name connections far worse than they group: human about 80% correct vs GPT-4 10-shot F1 41-45% and exact match under 15%; 8.2% of the model's connections wrongly include the clues themselves.
agent_test: Score the agent's stated reframing (the name of the hidden category) separately from the final answer.

claim: On MacGyver (1,683 problems; 1,306 solvable, 377 unsolvable; of the solvable, 1,073 = 82.2% need unconventional tool use) seven LLMs score 35-42% single-attempt vs 65.1% for average humans; majority of humans 79.3% vs GPT-4 73.3%; scale alone (Llama2 7B to 70B) gave no clear gain. One paper; about 6 human responses per problem, one random response used. Authors attribute most GPT-4 errors to physical infeasibility, not fixation (d09).
agent_test: Run the MacGyver 323-item subset with our scaffold vs plain vs best-of-N at equal tokens; report unsolvable-detection separately.

claim: GPT-4 errors on MacGyver: wrong tool usage 42.4%, not achieving the goal 17.7%, then hallucinations (unavailable tools 16.9% and unfaithful to constraints 9.5%, together 26.4%) per the paper text. Evidence lines c06 and b24 label rows differently; the paper text is used here.
agent_test: Tag agent failures into the same error types; G2 (verify against given constraints) should cut the hallucination types.

claim: Generic divergence or reflection prompts give small, model-dependent gains: MacGyver GPT-4 divergent-convergent +6.5 points efficient, self-reflect -9.7 points infeasible (180 items, single run); multi-agent debate raises GPT-3.5 counter-intuitive arithmetic 26.0% to 37.0% (200 items); entropy-gated reconsideration +8.41pp on MATH-500 (small open models). No confidence intervals; self-reflect failed for Claude2 and Llama2-13b.
agent_test: Run each prompt style at a fixed token budget with at least 3 seeds and report CIs; compare with plain resampling.

claim: Frontier-model fixation in clinical reasoning is contested. M-ARC (100 items): most LLMs under 50% vs 5 physicians 66% (SE 5.3). 2026 follow-up: Claude 4.1 Opus 0.751 (CI 0.738-0.763) and three other models level with physicians at high reasoning effort. MedEinst (5,383 cases, 17 LLMs): bias trap rates above 50% for several frontier models and no size link. Different benchmarks; M-ARC is public, so contamination is possible.
agent_test: Evaluate on a fresh unpublished set of misleading-prior cases; compare reasoning effort levels at equal tokens.

claim: Reasoning effort (not scale or few-shot) is what moves fixation-type scores: Shidara 2026 at highest effort; CresOWLve higher effort raised scores monotonically (GPT-5.4 nearly doubles). Against this: MedEinst GPT-5 trap rate 51.87% by the table, and few-shot did not help on Only Connect.
agent_test: Sweep thinking budget vs scaffold at equal tokens to see whether the scaffold beats extra raw thinking.

claim: Creative questions are harder than factual ones on the same knowledge base: CresOWLve (2,061 examples) drop of 6.08% (Gemini-3.1-Pro high) to 17.21% (Mistral-Large-3-675B) on the English set (re-verified in the PDF).
agent_test: Use as a harness check, not a causal claim; no human test.

claim: Vision-language models stay literal: on CREATE, wrong model answers described the images literally in 22.8% vs 8.9% for humans; text-only cues raised every model by 30.0-66.3 points; one model beat humans (32.5% vs 16.5% first attempt, human N=25). Model names unverifiable.
agent_test: If vision input is used, test whether naming the cue first (an S1 step) reproduces the text-cue gain.

claim: Models can beat humans on rebus-type puzzles: humans below GPT-4-turbo by 0.32 and GPT-4o by 0.39 (p<0.001), but above GPT-4 on Chinese character puzzles; models chose by reasoning (68.9-71.3%) where humans chose transformation (72.4%). This weakens a blanket 'LLMs are fixated' story.
agent_test: Separate puzzle types by whether the key move is a re-representation or a lookup.

claim: Spontaneous 'aha' reframing shifts in reasoning traces are rare and do not help by themselves: 6.31% of 1M+ traces (7.6% in one pool), no rise over GRPO training; only entropy-gated external reconsideration helped (+8.41pp on MATH-500, 0.3221 to 0.4062; re-verified). Small Qwen2.5 and Llama models. Gap check: DeepSeek-R1 and GPT-4o also show shifts in only about 1-7% of traces and no accuracy benefit (d08).
agent_test: Trigger O6 by uncertainty (entropy or disagreement across samples) rather than at fixed points; compare to always-on.

claim: Chain-of-thought removes perseveration on a card-sort task: WCST categories 0.3-0.5 standard prompt vs 4.6-5.0 with CoT (human 4.73, SD 0.45); perseverative errors did not fall uniformly. Executive control otherwise weak: flanker incongruent accuracy 40-60% vs human 93-96%.
agent_test: Run WCST-style rule-switch tasks with and without O6 at equal tokens.

claim: Underspecified multi-turn conversations cause early commitment: average 39% drop single to multi-turn over six tasks (200,000+ simulations); restating the whole context recovers only 15-20% of the drop.
agent_test: Test whether O6 plus a restatement of constraints recovers more than plain restatement.

claim: Exposure to generative AI output raises fixation in human designers: N=60 sketching study (GenAI negative on fluency about -0.21, originality negative with about 97% probability) and a 10-designer ChatGPT case study (novel-term share 67.4% vs 78.2%). Small effects, wide intervals.
agent_test: Human-side only; relevant to a multi-agent design where one agent's output anchors the next (G4).

claim: Consensus-style multi-agent systems can amplify the dominant prior: MDAgent and DyLAN on MedEinst have baseline accuracy 14.93% and 6.51% and trap rates about 40-42% (table reading; the paper text says robust accuracy about 8-10%, the table says 3.20 and 1.19, a conflict). Counter-evidence: forced-opposition debate with a judge raised GPT-3.5 counter-intuitive arithmetic 26.0 to 37.0 (d05); full-consensus prompts are a different design (d06). Token cost 2.46x, not matched.
agent_test: Compare single-agent O6 against debate at equal tokens on misleading-prior items.

claim: A metacognitive co-regulation loop (CRDAL) beat a plain loop in a battery design task: 141.17 vs 106.08 Ah (d=1.846, 30 runs each); reported numbers internally inconsistent for the self-regulation arm.
agent_test: Treat as a lead only; replicate on another task.

claim: Showing or naming the better alternative is not enough: in an eye-tracking cognitive-set task 89.6% of people did not adopt a visible shortcut, and after watching a video of it 29.4% (10 of 34) still did not use it, versus 70.6% who did. Set is a failure to try, not to see.
agent_test: O6 must include a forced trial with the alternative role (try it, check it), not only list it. Test: list-only vs list-then-attempt at equal tokens.

claim: Habit tendency did not predict classic candle-problem success (N=69, p=0.169; solvers few) but frequent past use of an object raised fluency and lowered flexibility of alternative uses. The candle item is a low-power probe of individual-difference fixation.
agent_test: Use alternative-use flexibility, not candle pass rate alone, as the fixation readout for the agent.

claim: Format changes that do not alter the representation do not help insight problems; information that exposes the misunderstanding does (physical matches no gain on the Pencil problem, N=87; matchstick picture gain on the arithmetic item).
agent_test: The S1 restate must expose structure (parts and their allowed roles), not only rephrase.

claim: Nine-dot difficulty is tied to lookahead and progress monitoring: simplified variants with stronger hints were solved by 80-93% while the nine-dot itself was solved by none (MacGregor, Ormerod and Chronicle 2001, Exp 1, secondary report only). No LLM run of nine-dot or matchstick problems was found.
agent_test: If tested, use nine-dot with and without hints on the agent; expect hints to matter more than naming.

claim: No published study was found that runs classic Luchins water-jar, candle, nine-dot or matchstick items on 2025-2026 LLMs, nor one that tests a naming scaffold against an equal-token plain baseline. Search tools were degraded (rate limits), so this is weak evidence of absence.
agent_test: Our own pilot on classic items is the only route to answer gaps 1-3.
